extracted_by: hand, T-0312 — the Democrat read, March 1834
note: Vol. I No. 17, and the month's most consequential single claim is written inside Fort Dearborn: a desertion notice dated at the post, signed by its adjutant and issued by order of a major, which shows the fort garrisoned and administered in March 1834 and dates enlistment there to the 1820s. Beside it, a new bakery opens on South Water Street a few doors north of Newberry & Dole — the only evidence in the month for where that forwarding house stood — three weeks after the town's old bakery closed; a benefit lecture on caloric is given in the Baptist Church at six on a Monday evening; a cabinet shop's benches, tools and cherry lumber are sold up; lots are advertised fronting on Kinzie and Michigan streets north of the river; and the bootmaker next door to Peter Cohen's store is legible here for the first time.

claims.notes: A PAID LECTURE ON HEAT, IN A CHURCH, AT SIX ON A MONDAY EVENING IN MARCH — and for a reconstruction the interesting word is EVENING. The Baptist Church has to be lit and warmed enough to hold a paying audience after dark at the end of a Chicago winter; the Presbyterian meeting house was shown doing the same for a temperance meeting in January (1834-01-28, claim c002 there). So both of the town's church buildings are documented as evening public rooms, which constrains their fabric more than a dedication notice does. THE SUBJECT IS 'CALORIC' — the fluid theory of heat, then still respectable — delivered by Dr. Temple, who is secretary of the Infant School's trustees three weeks earlier (1834-03-04, claim c016 there) and here its lecturer, with R. J. Hamilton the county clerk as president of the board and Maj. H. S. Handy, lately of the dissolved firm of Taylor & Handy, selling the tickets. Twenty-five cents at the door, the school's own children free. THE LECTURE'S DATE DIGIT IS BROKEN in the crop and is bracketed rather than supplied with confidence.

claims.notes: FORT DEARBORN IS GARRISONED, OCCUPIED AND ADMINISTERED IN MARCH 1834, and this notice is the proof from inside it. It is written at the fort, dated there — 'Fort Dearborn, March 20, 1834' — signed by a post adjutant, issued by order of a major, and it speaks of 'this Fort' and 'this Military Post' in the present tense. A post with an adjutant writing general orders is an ESTABLISHMENT, not a caretaker detachment, which matters because the second fort's condition and use in the years before the scene date is exactly the question the FORT tickets keep running into. IT ALSO DATES A CAREER: Morin 'was enlisted at Fort Dearborn, on the 8th December, 182[…]' — the year's last digits are lost to the crop and are NOT supplied, but the phrase places recruiting at this fort in the 1820s, before the second fort's 1832-33 reoccupation, and the man is still in its garrison in 1834. A SOLDIER WHO IS A CABINET MAKER is the third man in that trade this month, after A. Filer & Co. and W. Reed. THE COMMANDING OFFICER'S NAME IS NOT LEGIBLE: the transcription reads 'Maj, Garss' and no completion is asserted; nor is the adjutant identified further than the paper identifies him.

entities.role: baker on South Water Street, a few doors north of Newberry & Dole's store

claims.notes: A NEW BAKERY OPENING ON THE DAY THE PAPER WENT TO PRESS, AND IT PLACES TWO BUSINESSES AT ONCE. 'on South Water-street, a few doors north of Messrs. Newberry & Dole's store' is the only evidence in the entire month for where Newberry & Dole stood — their own advertisements give no address at all — so this notice puts the forwarding house on South Water Street by another man's reckoning, and the bakery a few doors up from it. THE TIMING IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE STORY. John Wellmaker's Man Trap, the town's bakery and confectioner's, closed on 4 March (1834-03-04, claims c011 and c031 there) and its partnership was dissolved in this same issue (claim c004 here). Three weeks after the old bakery shut, a new one opens on South Water Street. Nothing printed connects them and no connection is asserted — but the sequence is the kind of thing a month-long read is for, and a reconstruction that wants a working bakery on this street at the scene date now has a candidate with a documented opening. 'A FEW DOORS' IS NOT A NUMBER and is not treated as one; the placement carries the paper's own words. THE ADVERTISEMENT'S HEAD-LINE IS DESTROYED — the crop reads 'GMEORGO BARBEE-' above the signature — and is NOT reconstructed; only D. Graves's own name and text are read.

claims.notes: KINZIE AND MICHIGAN STREETS, NAMED AS FRONTAGES — two street names this corpus has not carried before, and both of them NORTH of the river, which is where the reconstruction's evidence thins fastest. Kinzie Street runs east and west along the north bank; Michigan Street (later Hubbard) lies a block north of it. Lots being advertised as 'fronting on' them in March 1834 means the streets existed as surveyed frontages by then, which is a different and weaker claim than saying they were made roads, and only the weaker one is made here. THE COUNT OF LOTS IS NOT LEGIBLE and is bracketed rather than supplied. THE POSTSCRIPT IS THE SECOND SCHOOL SECTION OFFER OF THE MONTH — 'Eight Blocks for sale in the School Section', beside P. Pruyne & Co.'s Lot No. 3 in Block 120 (1834-03-18, claim c006 there) — and eight whole blocks in one hand is a land holding, not a house lot. The seller is the same Dr. Temple who runs the Infant School's trustees and lectures for its benefit three days later.

claims.notes: A LOG HOUSE, A STABLE AND TWO THOUSAND RAILS, THIRTEEN MILES OUT — the countryside the town sat in, priced. This is outside the reconstruction's ground and is extracted anyway, because it is the only description in the month of what an ordinary improved claim in Cook county consisted of: a log house, a stable, about two thousand split rails lying ready for fencing, and a lot half timber and half high prairie. Two thousand rails is roughly a mile of worm fence, so the improvement is real and the seller is quantifying it. NO POSITION IS CLAIMED beyond the paper's own '13 miles from Chicago' and no direction is given or inferred. The seller is the postmaster, John S. C. Hogan, who in this same issue is also selling three hundred cedar posts (claim c010 here) — fencing timber, the other half of the same market. claims.notes: THE BOOTMAKER'S NAME, LEGIBLE AT LAST. On 4 March this advertisement sat inside the letter-list crop and its signature survived only as debris (1834-03-04, claim c026 there); here it reads 'MON TOOMERY' — Montgomery — and the person can be minted. The placement is unchanged and is the strongest anchor in the month: next door to P. Cohen's store, and Cohen's store is the one Chicago address in this corpus fixed on a SCAN-VERIFIED reading, at the east end of South Water Street (`data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json`). So a boot and shoe maker's shop stands at the east end of South Water Street from December 1833 through at least March 1834. THE INITIAL IS W, AND IT IS READ FROM THE JANUARY PRINTING OF THE IDENTICAL ADVERTISEMENT — 'W. MONTGOMERY. Chicago, Dec. 18, 1833' (1834-01-28, claim c008 there) — where the signature survives whole. THE TWO PRINTINGS DISAGREE ABOUT THE DATELINE'S DAY, 15 here against 18 there, and neither is preferred: both are OCR of the same broken type and the difference changes nothing that is claimed. Both printings are damaged in different places and the reading uses each where it is legible, keeping every quote to what its own column says. THE SIGNATURE IS LOTON W. MONTGOMERY'S, AND THE SHOEMAKING IS NOT THE AUCTIONEER'S (T-1040). This is ONE standing advertisement — 'Boot & Shoe Making. The subscriber having recently commenced the above business, next door to P. Cohen's Store …', the same setting word for word under a dateline of Chicago, December 1833 — and the Democrat runs it from 17 December 1833 through at least 8 April 1834. Four impressions bear on the signature and three of them carry an L: it is set WHOLE as 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' at 1833-12-17 c003 and at 1834-04-08 c007, and the damaged 1834-03-04 c028 preserves the initial itself — its column reads 'L.      Mo}' where the name stood. Those impressions stand on both sides of the two that read 'W. MONTGOMERY' (1834-01-28 c008, and 1834-03-25 c009, whose initial its own note says was READ FROM the January printing rather than off its own page). So the reading is L. W. Montgomery throughout, and `as_printed` is left exactly as each column sets it. WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not a merge of 'W. Montgomery' with 'L. W. Montgomery'. This corpus carries a real W. Montgomery — the auctioneer and commission merchant of South Water Street, signing 'W. MONTGOMERY' and 'W. MONTGOMERY, Auc'r.' across the summer of 1835 — and the identity policy's families rule rightly refuses to join two Montgomerys on a differing initial. The discriminator here is not the initial; it is that the shoemaking notice and the auction notices are two different advertisements, and this one is the shoemaker's. Before this ruling `person_w_montgomery` carried 'boot and shoe maker' beside 'auctioneer', 'commission merchant', 'land agent' and 'newspaper agent' — one record holding two men's trades on two signatures separated on the page. Loton W. Montgomery is in this reconstruction under his own name (hh_montgomery_l_w), on the polls of 1834 and 1835 and in Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844, a shoemaker in each.

claims.notes: WHAT THE TOWN COULD ACTUALLY BUY TO WEAR, IN ONE COLUMN. This is the longest goods list in the month and the reason to extract it whole is that it is a description of the town's CLOTHED APPEARANCE at a date: merino and Circassian cloths, Thibet and Prussian shawls, bandanna and Italian silk handkerchiefs, bobbinett lace, Marseilles and swansdown vestings, Irish linen, Canton flannel, scarlet and red flannels, indigo apron checks. A reconstruction that puts figures in a street can dress them from this and cite it. THE STOCK IS EASTERN AND IT IS FASHIONABLE, which is worth registering against the frontier picture: gros-de-Naples ribbon and figured bobbinett are not a trading-post inventory. The same merchant sells cut nails by the keg and holds the two buildings to let, so this is a general store of some size. NO ADDRESS IS GIVEN in this or in any of Wright's three March advertisements and none is inferred. The `lines_of_claim` omit only the transcription's own rules and blank separators.

claims.notes: THE SAME CALL, A DIFFERENT DAY — and both dates are kept. On 18 March this notice set the Cook county meeting for 'the 12th of April next, at the Eagle Hotel in Chicago, at 2 P. M.' (1834-03-18, claim c001 there); here, a week later, the same standing notice reads 'the 16th of [April]'. Nothing in either issue explains the change and neither reading is preferred over the other; what is claimed is that a county meeting was called to the Eagle Hotel in April 1834 and that the printed day moved. THE HOTEL IS THE POINT for this project: a second, independent printing confirms a named hotel in Chicago with a room that will take a public meeting, which is the sort of corroboration a single advertisement cannot give. THE CROP HAS CUT THIS COLUMN DOWN THE MIDDLE and interleaved it with the neighbouring editorial, so the `lines_of_claim` name only the lines carrying this notice and the normalized reading is completed from the 18 March printing of the identical text — completed, and marked as completed, never quoted from it.

claims.notes: A ST. JOSEPH FIRM, EXTRACTED BECAUSE OF WHO ITS PARTNER IS TO CHICAGO. Britain & Phelan is not a Chicago business and is not claimed as one — no `business` record is made for it here — but Calvin Britain is named in David Carver's standing advertisement as Carver's AGENT at St. Joseph, the man who forwards lumber and goods across the lake to Chicago (1834-03-04, claim c006 there), and Britain & Phelan stand in the same issues as a Buffalo mill-stone house's Michigan reference. So this notice documents the Michigan end of the supply chain that put timber, lath and shingles on Chicago's shore, and it dates a change in it: the partnership dissolved on 11 December 1833 with Phelan carrying it on. THE OTHER END OF THAT CHAIN IS ALSO IN THIS ISSUE, in the reference list of George W. Bush & Co. of Buffalo, where 'J. H. Kinzie, Chicago' stands among the western houses. Neither man is placed in Chicago and neither is claimed to be.
